q: Which Azure Policy effect blocks a non-compliant resource from being created?
exp: Deny evaluates the request before the resource is created or updated, and rejects it if it breaks the rule, so the non-compliant resource never exists. Audit and AuditIfNotExists only report, and Append adds fields to the request rather than blocking it.

q: You need every new resource group to have a 'costcenter' tag, and creation must fail if it's missing. Which built-in policy and effect?
opts: Require a tag on resource groups — Deny
Inherit a tag from the subscription — Modify
exp: The built-in 'Require a tag on resource groups' policy uses the Deny effect, so creating a resource group without the costcenter tag fails. 'Inherit a tag' (Modify) copies a tag that already exists rather than enforcing it, Append adds a value instead of failing, and 'Allowed locations' is about regions.

q: Which effect adds or replaces tags on resources during creation or update, and supports remediation of existing resources?
exp: Modify can add, replace or remove tags (and some other properties) while a resource is being created or updated. For resources that already exist, a remediation task applies the change through the assignment's managed identity. Audit only reports, Deny blocks, and Disabled turns the policy off.

q: You must restrict VM sizes to the D-series only. Which built-in policy?
exp: The built-in 'Allowed virtual machine size SKUs' policy takes a list of permitted sizes, such as the D-series, and denies deployments of any other size. 'Allowed locations' restricts regions, and the resource-type policies allow or block whole resource types rather than sizes.

q: You must prevent anyone from creating public IP addresses in a subscription. Simplest built-in policy?
exp: The built-in 'Not allowed resource types' policy denies any deployment of the resource types you list. Listing Microsoft.Network/publicIPAddresses stops anyone creating public IPs in that scope. 'Allowed locations' and 'Require a tag' don't block a resource type.

q: An assignment uses DeployIfNotExists. The remediation task fails with an authorization error. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The policy's managed identity lacks the required role assignment at the target scope
The policy is in Audit mode
Resource locks are missing, so the remediation task can't protect the target scope
exp: DeployIfNotExists and Modify remediations run as the policy assignment's managed identity. If that identity doesn't have the needed role (for example Contributor) at the target scope, the remediation fails with an authorization error. Audit mode, locks and budgets aren't involved.

q: How often does Azure Policy run a standard compliance evaluation for already-assigned policies?
exp: Azure Policy evaluates resources when they're created or updated, when an assignment is created or changed, and in a standard compliance scan every 24 hours. You can also start an on-demand scan, for example with az policy state trigger-scan.

q: Which command triggers an on-demand policy compliance scan for a resource group?
exp: az policy state trigger-scan starts an on-demand compliance evaluation for a subscription or, with --resource-group, one resource group (in PowerShell: Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan). Without it you wait for the 24-hour cycle. The other commands don't exist.

q: At which scopes can a policy be assigned?
opts: Management group, subscription, or resource group
Entra ID tenant, administrative unit, or security group
exp: Policy assignments target management groups, subscriptions or resource groups and apply to everything below. Child resource groups or individual resources can be excluded from an assignment.

q: What's the difference between a policy exclusion and a policy exemption?
opts: An exclusion removes a scope from evaluation entirely; an exemption keeps it evaluated but marks it Exempt
An exemption removes a scope from evaluation entirely; an exclusion keeps it evaluated but hides it from reports
exp: An exclusion removes a scope from the assignment completely, so it isn't evaluated at all. An exemption keeps the scope evaluated but marks it as Exempt, with a category (Waiver or Mitigated) and an optional expiry date, so it stays visible in compliance reports.

q: You want compliance results without blocking anything during a pilot of a Deny policy. What's the fastest option?
opts: Set the assignment's enforcement mode to DoNotEnforce
Set the assignment's scope to the tenant root management group
exp: Setting an assignment's enforcementMode to DoNotEnforce makes Azure Policy evaluate resources and report compliance, but it doesn't block anything. That lets you see what a Deny policy would affect before enforcing it. Deleting the policy gives you no results at all, and locks are unrelated.

q: Which effect checks whether a related resource exists (e.g., an antimalware extension on a VM) and only reports?
exp: AuditIfNotExists checks whether a related resource exists — such as an extension on a VM or a diagnostic setting on a resource — and marks the resource non-compliant if it doesn't. It only reports. DeployIfNotExists would also deploy the missing resource, and Deny blocks requests.

q: Which TWO effects can be remediated with a remediation task?
exp: Only DeployIfNotExists and Modify can change resources after the fact, so only they support remediation tasks for existing non-compliant resources. Audit only reports, and Deny only blocks new requests; neither has anything to remediate.

q: You need to enforce ISO 27001-style controls using dozens of policies. What's the most efficient approach?
opts: Assign a built-in initiative (policy set) once
Assign each policy individually to every subscription
exp: An initiative groups many policy definitions, so assigning one built-in initiative (for example a regulatory compliance standard) applies dozens of controls in one step and gives one compliance score. Assigning each policy separately is far more work, and locks and Advisor don't enforce compliance controls.

q: Policy A (assigned at the subscription) denies East US. Policy B (assigned at RG1) allows only East US. Can anyone create a resource in RG1?
opts: Yes, in East US — the RG-level policy wins, because it's closer to the resource
No — both policies are evaluated; any location in RG1 is denied by one of them
exp: Policies are cumulative — a lower-scope policy can't override a higher one. In RG1, East US is denied by Policy A, and every other region is denied by Policy B. So nothing can be created in RG1, whatever the user's role.

q: Which policy definition parameter technique makes one definition reusable with different allowed values per assignment?
exp: Policy parameters let one definition take different values for each assignment — for example a list of allowed locations that's different for each subscription. Aliases map to resource properties, and tags and locks aren't policy features.

q: Answer Yes or No about Azure Policy:
stmts: A Deny policy applies even to users with the Owner role
Policy can evaluate resource properties such as SKU or location
Policy assignments at a management group inherit to child subscriptions
Policy controls who can sign in to Azure
exp: A Deny policy applies to everyone, including Owners, because Policy checks the request, not the user. It can evaluate properties such as SKU or location, and assignments at a management group are inherited by its subscriptions. Policy doesn't control who can sign in — that's Conditional Access.

q: Order the steps to enforce allowed locations on a subscription and fix tags on existing resources with a Modify policy:
items: Create a remediation task for the Modify assignment
Assign 'Allowed locations' with Deny at the subscription
Assign the Modify tag policy with a managed identity
exp: First assign the Deny policy so new resources outside the allowed locations are blocked. Then assign the Modify tag policy with a managed identity, because remediation acts as that identity. Next run a remediation task to fix existing resources. Finally check the compliance dashboard to confirm the result.

q: You want to prevent accidental deletion of a production SQL server, but admins must still scale it. Which lock?
exp: A CanNotDelete lock stops anyone deleting the server but still allows changes such as scaling. A ReadOnly lock would also block scaling. Giving admins only Reader would stop them scaling too, and a Deny policy controls how resources are configured, not whether they can be deleted.

q: A ReadOnly lock is applied to an App Service plan. What happens when you try to scale out the plan?
opts: It fails — scaling is a write operation
exp: A ReadOnly lock allows only read (GET) operations. Scaling out an App Service plan changes its configuration, which is a write, so it fails until the lock is removed. That applies to manual scaling and autoscale alike.

q: A CanNotDelete lock exists on a resource group. Can you delete the resource group with the Owner role?
exp: A CanNotDelete lock on a resource group blocks deleting it (and the resources in it) for every user, Owners included. Remove the lock first — Owners have permission to do that — then delete. There's no --force flag that bypasses locks.

q: Which CLI command creates a delete lock on resource group RG1?
opts: az lock create --name NoDelete --lock-type CanNotDelete --resource-group RG1
az policy lock create --name NoDelete --effect Deny --resource-group RG1 --force
exp: az lock create --lock-type CanNotDelete --resource-group RG1 creates a delete lock on the resource group (use ReadOnly for a read-only lock). The other commands aren't real; az policy creates policies, not locks.

q: A ReadOnly lock is on a VM's resource group. Users report they can't start the VM. Why?
opts: Start is a POST action, and ReadOnly allows only reads
A ReadOnly lock deallocates the VM and releases its compute
exp: Starting a VM is a POST action (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/start/action). ReadOnly locks allow only GET requests, so the start fails, along with restart and deallocate. Remove the lock or use CanNotDelete if VMs need to keep running normally.

q: Answer Yes or No about locks:
stmts: Locks apply to data-plane operations such as writing blobs
A lock on a subscription is inherited by all resource groups
CanNotDelete still allows resource configuration changes
exp: Locks apply only to control-plane operations, so data operations such as writing blobs still work. A lock on a subscription is inherited by every resource group. CanNotDelete still allows configuration changes. Contributor can't remove locks, because it doesn't have Microsoft.Authorization/locks permissions.

q: What's the maximum number of tag name/value pairs per resource?
exp: Each resource, resource group and subscription supports up to 50 tag name/value pairs. That's a platform limit, so 15, 100 and unlimited are wrong. If you need more data, store it in one tag value as JSON.

q: Finance wants monthly cost reports grouped by department. What's the simplest setup?
opts: Tag resources with department and group by that tag in Cost analysis
Create a budget per department and group by that budget in Azure Advisor
exp: Tag resources with a key such as department, then use Cost Management → Cost analysis and group or filter by that tag to get spend per department. Separate subscriptions per resource is impractical, locks don't affect costs, and budgets alert on spend rather than report it by department.

q: Which role lets a user manage tags on resources WITHOUT access to the resources themselves?
exp: Tag Contributor can add, change and remove tags on resources without any other access to them. Contributor would give full control of the resources, Reader can't change tags, and User Access Administrator manages role assignments.

q: Which CLI command adds tag env=prod to an existing resource group without removing other tags?
exp: az tag update with --operation Merge adds env=prod and keeps any existing tags. --operation Replace would remove every tag not listed. az group update --tags sets the whole tag list, so it can remove tags rather than merge them. The other commands don't exist.

q: In Cost Management, which feature applies subscription and resource group tags to child resource usage records for reporting?
exp: Cost Management's tag inheritance setting applies subscription and resource group tags to the usage records of child resources, so cost reports can group by them. It doesn't change the resources. Policy Deny blocks deployments, and locks and budgets don't handle tags.

q: What happens to the resources when you delete a resource group?
opts: They are moved to the default RG
exp: A resource group is a lifecycle container: deleting it deletes every resource inside it — VMs, disks, networks and everything else. Nothing is moved elsewhere or left behind, which is why delete locks on important resource groups are a good idea.

q: Can a resource group in West Europe contain a VM deployed in East US?
opts: No — a VM's region must match its resource group
Yes — the RG location only stores metadata
exp: A resource group's location only says where its metadata is stored. The resources inside can be in any region, so a West Europe resource group can hold a VM in East US. Regions don't have to match, and peering has nothing to do with this.

q: Can a single resource belong to two resource groups at the same time?
opts: No — a resource belongs to exactly one resource group
Yes — if both resource groups are in the same region
exp: Every resource belongs to exactly one resource group at a time. You can move it to another resource group, but it can't be in two at once. Tags let you group resources across resource groups for reporting, without changing where they live.

q: Before moving resources to another subscription, how do you check whether the move will succeed without performing it?
opts: Run what-if on an ARM template
exp: Azure can validate a move without doing it: the portal runs validation when you start a move, and the validateMoveResources API (az resource invoke-action --action validateMoveResources) checks that all resources and dependencies can move. What-if previews template deployments, not moves.

q: Which is required for moving resources to a different subscription?
opts: Source and destination subscriptions must be in the same Entra tenant and the resource provider must be registered in the destination
The destination subscription must be empty and in the same region as the source, and all resources must be stopped before the move
exp: To move resources to another subscription, both subscriptions must be in the same Microsoft Entra tenant, and the destination must have the resource provider registered (for example Microsoft.Compute). The destination doesn't need to be empty, and no Entra licence is needed.

q: Which CLI command moves a resource to another resource group?
exp: az resource move --destination-group RG2 --ids <resource IDs> moves one or more resources to another resource group (add --destination-subscription-id to change subscription). The other commands don't exist. During the move, both resource groups are locked.

q: Your deployment fails with 'QuotaExceeded' for vCPUs in a region. What do you do?
opts: Request a quota increase in Usage + quotas
Move the subscription to a different Entra tenant
exp: vCPU quotas are set per region and per subscription. When a deployment hits the limit, request an increase in Subscription → Usage + quotas (or Help + support). Locks, tenant changes and budgets don't change quotas.

q: Deployment fails with 'The subscription is not registered to use namespace Microsoft.ContainerInstance'. Fix?
exp: Before using a resource type, its resource provider must be registered in the subscription. Running az provider register --namespace Microsoft.ContainerInstance (or Resource providers → Register in the portal) fixes the error. It isn't about licences, management groups or policies.

q: Why would an organization use multiple subscriptions?
opts: To separate billing, enforce boundaries for quotas and access, and isolate environments (prod/dev)
Subscriptions are free to create without billing
To meet the Azure requirement that production VMs, storage accounts and VNets live in separate subscriptions
exp: Subscriptions are boundaries for billing (one invoice each), for scale (quotas apply per subscription) and for management (RBAC and policies can be assigned per subscription). That makes them good for separating production from development. Subscriptions aren't free, and VMs don't need their own subscription.

q: What is the main purpose of management groups?
opts: Manage access, policy, and compliance across multiple subscriptions
Group users and devices for licensing across multiple tenants
exp: Management groups sit above subscriptions. Anything you assign to one — RBAC roles or Azure Policy — is inherited by every subscription under it, so you can govern many subscriptions with one assignment. They don't hold VMs, DNS zones or users.

q: How many parent management groups can a subscription have?
exp: A management group hierarchy is a tree, so every subscription and management group has exactly one parent. A subscription can't belong to two management groups at the same time; you move it from one to another.

q: By default, where are new subscriptions placed in the management group hierarchy?
exp: New subscriptions go under the tenant root group by default. In the hierarchy settings you can choose a different default management group, so new subscriptions land somewhere with the right policies. There's no group automatically called 'Default'.

q: Approximately how many management groups can a single directory support?
exp: One Microsoft Entra directory can hold up to 10,000 management groups, in a hierarchy up to six levels deep (not counting the root and subscriptions). That's far more than most organisations need.

q: Order the steps to apply one 'Allowed locations' policy to 12 subscriptions with the least effort:
items: Assign the 'Allowed locations' policy at the management group
exp: Create the management group, move the 12 subscriptions under it, and then assign the policy once at the management group. Inheritance applies it to all 12 subscriptions. Finally check compliance. Assigning first would work too, but moving the subscriptions before assigning keeps the order logical and nothing is missed.

q: You want an email and a webhook call when actual spend reaches 90% of a monthly budget. What do you configure?
opts: A budget with an alert condition at 90% using an action group
An Azure Policy with an Audit effect at 90% of the monthly spend
exp: A budget in Cost Management can have alert conditions, such as Actual at 90%. Each condition can email recipients and trigger an action group, which can call a webhook, Logic App or runbook. Policy, locks and Advisor don't track spend against a budget.

q: Which tool provides recommendations such as resizing or shutting down underutilized VMs to save money?
exp: Azure Advisor's Cost recommendations find idle or underused resources, suggest resizing or shutting down VMs, and recommend reservations. Policy enforces rules, Network Watcher diagnoses networking, and Service Health reports Azure incidents.

q: Azure Advisor gives recommendations in which categories?
opts: Cost, Security, Reliability, Operational excellence, Performance
Identity, Compliance, Networking, Licensing, and Data protection
exp: Azure Advisor gives recommendations in five categories: Reliability, Security, Performance, Cost and Operational Excellence — the pillars of the Azure Well-Architected Framework. It isn't limited to cost and security.

q: A VM runs 24/7 for the next three years with a stable size. Which option reduces compute cost the most?
opts: Azure Spot VMs with a deallocate eviction policy
exp: A 3-year reserved instance gives the biggest discount for a VM that runs all the time at a stable size. Pay-as-you-go is the most expensive, Spot VMs can be evicted at any time (unsuitable for 24/7 work), and a bigger VM costs more.

q: You want to reuse existing on-premises Windows Server licenses with Software Assurance on Azure VMs. Which benefit?
exp: Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you use existing Windows Server (or SQL Server) licences that have Software Assurance on Azure VMs, so you pay only for the base compute rate. Reserved instances discount compute for a 1- or 3-year commitment, and Spot and Dev/Test are different pricing options.

q: Before deploying, you need to estimate the monthly cost of 3 VMs and a storage account. Which tool?
exp: The Azure pricing calculator estimates the cost of services you plan to deploy, such as 3 VMs and a storage account. The TCO calculator compares on-premises costs with Azure, and Cost analysis and Advisor work on resources that already exist.

ctx: MG-Root → MG-Prod → Sub-Prod → RG-Web (tag env=prod) → WebApp1. Policy 'Inherit tag env from resource group' (Modify) is assigned at MG-Prod. Bob has Reader at MG-Root. A ReadOnly lock is on RG-Web.
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: A new App Service created in RG-Web gets env=prod automatically
An Owner of Sub-Prod can change WebApp1's app settings without removing the lock
Moving Sub-Prod under another MG removes the inherited policy from its resources
exp: The ReadOnly lock blocks creating a new App Service in RG-Web, so nothing gets tagged; Reader inherits from root; ReadOnly blocks writes even for Owner; policy follows hierarchy placement, so moving the subscription out of MG-Prod removes it.
